title: Stolen Car Leads to 5-Star Wanted Level Chase
description:
Submit a tip! Tips@Midwest-Safety.com

Please consider JOINING for $1 a month. It *really* helps us do original reporting like this. 

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com

transcript.text: On September 17th, 2003, Lake County deputies in Florida got behind a stolen Toyota Corolla. The felony stop wouldn't go as planned, and Deputy Corey Lebrecht, along with his K-9 Murphy, would take the lead in the moments ahead. Yolson, let's take it in the intersection. Let's block it in. What? We're on South Street. Eagle One's going to call it. I'm number one. Aggravated battery on Leo. At this point, officers back off. Eagle One, Lake County's helicopter, has the suspect in view from above. For the next several minutes, the chase goes quiet. Eventually, Eagle One spots the vehicle turning into a dead-end neighborhood. Deputies close in, setting up stop sticks and preparing to box him in. Justin's sticks. He's going to just ram us. Completely past the front, passenger back, both rooms. Good boy. Good boy. Good boy. Good job, Murph. Nothing. This pants. Yeah, I saw him his pants. Good job, Murphy. Good job, buddy. Here, Murphy. Okay, why don't my hair clothes? He'll be my rights or nothing. You should put the lights on this. Passinger side? Yeah, I see. I didn't get out. He didn't do a whole lot of damage. I could just scrape the side. The suspect, 26-year-old Henry Lee Gamble Coleman, was taken into custody after a K-9 apprehension. He was charged with Grand Theft Auto, aggravated battery on law enforcement, and fleeing to elude. His bond was set at $16,000. While records don't show a sentencing for this incident, he was booked again in May, 2024 on charges, including resisting without violence, possession of a controlled substance and sexual battery. All suspects are innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Ever wonder what kind of mindset makes someone hit the gas and brought daylight while sitting in a stolen car? Suns out and life is normal and the person still decides the smartest thing to do is play a game with cops that they weren't built to win. Thieves rarely plan their escape. They improvise on the fly and these people driving away that tell you they're not thinking ahead even five seconds. Daylight makes every choice louder, every mistake clear, and every decision they make impossible to miss. You can see it in the way they maneuvered the car, no plan just reacting to whatever's in front of them. But this is what's good about daywork because it doesn't hide anything. It shows you every bad decision as it happens. After a while as a cop, you can spot when someone's just trying to outrun the mess they made. Even with the tires shredded down to nothing, this guy still tried to drag that car forward like a few more feet was going to outsmart with probably a lifetime of bad decisions. Now, he jumped out of that car like he had one last genius move left in him, but that move lasted about 10 seconds. Because the K-9 didn't hesitate. That dog locked onto him the way a well-trained partner does. No confusion, no doubt, just purpose. And watching this guy go from, I got this to I'm done, is one of the reasons cops do this job. The way these criminals are wired is truly something to be studied because they'll risk a car, a dog bite, and their own freedom long before they'll risk being honest about the life that got them here.
